key_terms.meaning: A predicate names a property or a relation; Reads(x, y) is true when x reads y.
A constant names one fixed individual, such as Chennai or Meera.
A variable ranges over individuals and is bound by ∀ (for all) or ∃ (there exists).
A entails B when every situation that makes A true also makes B true.
The terminology half of a description-logic knowledge base: concepts, roles and their axioms.
The assertion half of a description-logic knowledge base: facts about named individuals, like Father(Ramesh).
An event is an extra argument, so Ramesh ate idli at 8 becomes ∃e (Eat(e, Ramesh, idli) ∧ At(e, 8)).
A family of decidable fragments of first-order logic built from concepts, roles and individuals.
A rule attached to a grammar rule that builds the meaning of the mother node from the meanings of its daughters.
One word form carrying several related senses, as bank of a river and bank for money.
The is-a relation between senses: car is a hyponym of vehicle, vehicle is its hypernym.
Senses with opposite meaning, either gradable (hot–cold) or complementary (dead–alive).
The most specific synset that is an ancestor of both synsets in the WordNet hierarchy.
The part-of relation between senses: wheel is a meronym of car.
The fixed list of senses a word is allowed to take in a word sense disambiguation system.
Labels such as Agent, Patient and Goal that say what each argument does in the event a predicate names.
Constraints a predicate places on its arguments, for example Eat wants a living Agent and a solid Food.
The surface ties — reference, ellipsis, substitution, conjunction, lexical repetition — that hold a text together.
In Rhetorical Structure Theory, the central span of a relation (nucleus) and the span that supports it (satellite).
Two mentions that point to the same real-world entity, as Meera in sentence 1 and she in sentence 4.

takeaways: A meaning representation must be unambiguous, canonical and expressive enough for the computer to draw inferences.
First-order logic gives predicates, constants, variables and quantifiers; description logics cut expressiveness to keep reasoning decidable.
Davidson's event variable turns time, place and manner into separate predicates over one event.
Semantic attachments make meaning compositional: the parse tree builds the logical form rule by rule from the leaves up.
Word senses are linked by stable relations, and WordNet stores them as a graph whose nodes are synsets.
FrameNet describes meaning through frames and frame elements, which is closer to an event scene than a list of words.
Word sense disambiguation needs three things: a sense inventory, a context window, and evidence from a dictionary or from labelled data.
Thematic roles and selectional restrictions turn a predicate's argument list into a small scene with expected fillers.
Discourse is coherent through relations between segments and cohesive through surface ties; segmentation finds the spans that carry these links.
Coreference resolution groups mentions of one entity; anaphora resolution picks the single antecedent a pronoun depends on.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually marked for a formal definition plus a worked example on a given sentence — building a logical form, running a disambiguation or similarity step, and then judging which approach suits a named application such as information extraction or question answering.

bank.q: What is a meaning representation? List the properties a good meaning representation should have and explain each with an example.
outline: Definition: a formal language that stores sentence meaning and supports inference
Unambiguity: one sentence gets one representation
Canonical form: paraphrases map to the same representation
Expressiveness versus tractability trade-off
Inferencing: support for entailment and query answering
One worked example showing synonym sentences collapsing to one form

bank.q: Explain description logics. Distinguish the TBox from the ABox and show how a small knowledge base is written and queried.
outline: Concepts, roles and individuals
TBox holds terminological axioms such as Car ⊑ Vehicle
ABox holds assertions such as Owns(Meera, WagonR)
Subsumption and instance checking as the two reasoning services
Why DL is decidable while full first-order logic is not

bank.q: Define synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy and meronymy, giving two examples of each from everyday English or an Indian language.
outline: Synonymy: senses that can substitute without change of meaning; near-synonyms differ in connotation
Antonymy: gradable versus complementary pairs
Hyponymy: is-a hierarchy with hypernym and hyponym
Meronymy: part-of and its inverse holonymy
Why these relations matter for similarity and inference

bank.q: Explain coherence and cohesion in discourse. Describe the five cohesion devices with one example each.
outline: Coherence: the text makes sense as a whole through discourse relations
Cohesion: surface ties between sentences
Reference: pronoun or demonstrative pointing to an earlier mention
Ellipsis and substitution: leaving out or replacing a repeated phrase
Conjunction: and, but, because linking clauses
Lexical cohesion: repetition, synonymy and collocation

bank.q: Define semantic roles and selectional restrictions. Give a sentence and label its arguments with roles, then state the restrictions its predicate imposes.
outline: Role labels: Agent, Patient, Experiencer, Goal, Instrument, Source
Roles are verb-specific but drawn from a small inventory
Selectional restriction as a constraint on the filler of a slot
Example: Eat wants an animate Agent and a solid Food
Use in parsing, word sense disambiguation and information extraction

bank.q: Write the first-order logic form of Every student reads a book, then give its Davidson-style event representation for the sentence Meera read the newspaper in Chennai at 7 a.m.
outline: Correct use of ∀, ∃ and implication for quantified sentences
∀x (Student(x) → ∃y (Book(y) ∧ Reads(x, y)))
Event variable: ∃e (Read(e, Meera, newspaper) ∧ In(e, Chennai) ∧ At(e, 7 a.m.))
Explanation that each modifier becomes a separate conjunct, avoiding new predicate arities
Note on quantifier scope ambiguity in the first sentence

bank.q: Write the grammar rules with semantic attachments needed to compute the logical form of every student reads a book, and show the logical form built at each node of the parse tree.
outline: Rule-to-rule hypothesis: each syntactic rule carries one attachment
NP → Det N with lambda expressions for determiners
VP → V NP producing a lambda abstraction
S → NP VP applying the subject meaning to the VP meaning
Tree walk showing the form assembled bottom-up
Where the quantifier scope ambiguity appears

bank.q: Apply the Lesk algorithm by hand to disambiguate bank in the sentence The fisherman sat on the bank of the river and pulled out a fish. Show the glosses compared and the overlap counts.
outline: State the sense inventory with dictionary glosses for the two senses
Choose the context window
List the content words of the context
Count overlapping words between context and each gloss
Pick the sense with the higher overlap and state the answer
Mention extended Lesk and its use of related words

bank.q: Using WordNet, compute the path-length similarity and the lowest-common-subsumer similarity between two synsets, and explain why the two measures can rank the same pair differently.
outline: Path length: number of edges between the synsets, similarity = 1/(1+length)
LCS: deepest synset that is an ancestor of both
Depth-based formula such as 2·depth(LCS)/(depth(s1)+depth(s2))
Worked numbers on one concrete pair
Path length ignores where the pair sits in the hierarchy, LCS uses depth, so the rankings differ

bank.q: Take a short four-sentence paragraph and build its coreference chains: mark every mention, list the anaphors and their antecedents, and note the cases where a rule-based resolver would fail.
outline: Mention detection for noun phrases, pronouns and proper names
Separate coreference chains for each entity
Antecedent chosen by number, gender and recency agreement
Failures: ambiguous pronouns, cataphora, bridged references, metaphors
Statement of the evaluation measures used for such a system

bank.q: Compare dictionary-based, supervised and bootstrapping approaches to word sense disambiguation. State when each is the right choice and what limits its accuracy.
outline: Dictionary and thesaurus methods: Lesk, extended Lesk, no training data needed, gloss overlap is weak evidence
Supervised methods: features from a context window, Naive Bayes or logistic regression, needs a sense-annotated corpus
Bootstrapping and co-training: small seed set, self-labelled data, risk of semantic drift
Domain dependence and the low baseline set by the most frequent sense
Evaluation by precision, recall and F1 against a sense inventory
Practical recommendation for a language with few annotated corpora

bank.q: Discuss the limits of first-order logic as a meaning representation. Cover expressiveness, decidability, quantifier scope and the use of events and description logics as responses.
outline: What FOL captures well: relations, quantifiers, inference by entailment
Undecidability of full FOL and the practical cost of theorem proving
Quantifier scope ambiguity and the need for a canonical form
Davidson's event argument as a fix for variable-arity predicates
Description logics as a decidable fragment for large knowledge bases
Domain models and ontologies in real deployments

bank.q: WordNet or FrameNet? Evaluate the two lexical knowledge networks for an information extraction task and justify which one you would use for extracting who ate what at a wedding.
outline: WordNet: synsets, synset identifiers, relations, glosses, multilingual linking
Strength: sense inventory and similarity measures for words
FrameNet: frames, frame elements, lexical units, annotated example sentences
Strength: role structure of an event, directly usable as extraction template
Weakness of WordNet for role structure, weakness of FrameNet for word-level similarity
Decision for the extraction task, with a hybrid option

bank.q: Explain Rhetorical Structure Theory: nucleus and satellite, common rhetorical relations, and how a discourse tree is built for a short text. Discuss how segmentation errors affect the tree.
outline: Discourse units from segmentation cues
Nucleus carries the main claim, satellite supports it
Relations such as Elaboration, Contrast, Cause, Background
Composition of relations into a binary tree
Segmentation errors propagate upward
Coherence versus cohesion and where each shows in the tree

bank.q: Explain anaphora and coreference resolution. Compare rule-based, mention-ranking and neural approaches, and discuss the special difficulties for Indian languages and for metaphorical text.
outline: Terms: anaphor, antecedent, cataphora, coreference chain
Rule-based: agreement, recency, syntactic binding constraints
Mention ranking: features scored pairwise, or a classifier over candidate pairs
Neural and embedding-based models: contextual representations of mentions
Indian language issues: free word order, pro-drop, rich morphology, fewer annotated corpora
Metaphor and zero pronouns as remaining hard cases
Evaluation with the standard coreference metrics

glossary.def: A set of word forms that share one sense in WordNet, such as {car, auto, automobile}.
The more general sense in a hyponymy pair; vehicle is the hypernym of car.
The whole in a part-of relation; car is the holonym of wheel.
Two unrelated senses that happen to share a word form, as the two nouns bank.
The property that a text makes sense as a whole because its sentences are linked by discourse relations.
A mention that depends on an earlier mention for its meaning, as a pronoun depends on a name.
An anaphor that appears before the mention it depends on.
The earlier mention that an anaphor refers back to.
A word sense disambiguation method that picks the dictionary sense whose gloss overlaps most with the context words.
Training that starts from a small seed set and adds the system's own confident predictions as new labelled data.
A role inside a FrameNet frame, such as Eater and Food for the Ingestion frame.
Similarity computed from the contexts in which two words occur, without using a dictionary.
Describing one thing in terms of another, so the intended meaning goes beyond the literal senses of the words.
A contiguous stretch of text treated as one unit for coherence analysis.
The order in which ∀ and ∃ are applied, which changes the truth conditions of a sentence.
A named link between two discourse segments, such as Elaboration or Contrast.
The fixed number of words on each side of a target word that a disambiguation system uses as evidence.
A word form treated as one vocabulary item, carrying its own set of senses.
The task of assigning a thematic role to each argument of a predicate in a sentence.
Meaning that depends on context and speaker intention, over and above literal sentence meaning.
A formal, shared description of the concepts in a domain and the relations among them.
A set of WordNets for different languages whose synsets are linked by shared identifiers.
